items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

items.title: Stop Cursor Forgetting Your Database Schema (EF Core Guide)
items.summary: Ask Cursor for a query against a table it touched yesterday and it may still guess the column name, invent a navigation property, or write a migration for a column that already exists. It looks like forgetting. It's actually something simpler: the agent never had your schema in the first place, and every new chat starts empty. This guide shows how to put an accurate, compact version of your EF Core schema where the agent will read it, keep it from going stale, and make your project rules stick at the same time. Language models don't retain memory between sessions; Cursor's own docs say so plainly, and that's why rules exist. Within a session, the agent only knows what it has read. On an EF Core codebase, the schema is spread across places it rarely reads together: Entity classes give property names, which are not necessarily column names. Fluent configuration (IEntityTypeConfiguration , OnModelCreating) renames tables and columns, sets keys, owned types, value conversions and query filters. Conventions decide everything nobody configured explicitly, and they're invisible in the code. Migrations record how the schema got here, across dozens of files the agent has no reason to open.

items.title: Cursor for C# and .NET in 2026: Extensions, Debugging, Unity
items.summary: The first hour of C# in Cursor is more confusing than it should be. You open a solution, Cursor offers extensions you've never heard of, the one you use in VS Code isn't there, and the debugger behaves slightly differently. None of it is hard once you know why. This guide covers the licensing reason behind it, the three C# extensions that do work, a debugging setup that holds up on real solutions, Unity projects, and the rules that make Cursor write C# the way your team does. Cursor is built on the open-source VS Code codebase, but several of Microsoft's most popular extensions are not open source. The C# Dev Kit, the official C# extension's proprietary pieces and the vsdbg debugger are licensed for use only in Microsoft products: Visual Studio, VS Code and their hosted variants. Since Microsoft tightened enforcement in April 2025, opening a C# project in a fork showed a message that the extension may be used only with Microsoft Visual Studio Code. Cursor's response was to rebuild the affected extensions on open alternatives. In May 2025 it published its own C# extension (publisher: Anysphere), with one notable swap: debugging uses Samsung's open-source netcoredbg instead of vsdbg.

items.title: How to verify webhook HMAC signatures in PHP and Node.js
items.summary: A webhook endpoint is a public URL that changes orders. Anyone who finds it can send it a request that says "invoice paid", so the only thing standing between a forged request and a shipped order is the signature check. This post builds that check in PHP and in Node.js, step by step, and runs it against a valid request, a forged one and a replayed one. The examples use the Stablevoy header format, X-Stablevoy-Signature: t= ,v1= . Many payment providers sign webhooks the same way and differ only in the header name and the encoding, so the code carries over with small changes. The sender and your server share one secret. The sender never sends it: it uses the secret to compute an HMAC of the request and puts the result in a header. Your server computes the same HMAC from what it received. If the two match, the request came from someone who knows the secret and nobody changed it on the way. One delivery. A request without a 2xx answer in time is sent again, so the same event can arrive more than once. Two things follow from this picture. items.title: Node.js Multipart Object Storage for AI Images: A 2-Path Production Design
items.summary: Short answer: use private object storage with multipart upload for large AI-generated images, and make retention plus deletion an application-owned workflow. A single PUT is fine for a small thumbnail; it is the wrong default for a 300 MB image set or a zip export from a logistics tenant. The system I would ship has two viable shapes. In the direct shape, a Node.js worker streams bytes to storage and the API owns the multipart session. In the brokered shape, the worker asks the API for signed part URLs, uploads parts without proxying every byte through the app, then records the completed object in a database. Both shapes keep buckets private and return signed retrieval URLs. The invariant is the same: an export is visible only after completion, and every upload session ends with either complete or abort. Infrai fits the brokered version when a small team wants one REST API, one key, and one bill for storage alongside other backend capabilities. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples also mean the worker can use plain HTTP without installing a storage SDK. items.summary: Imagine a customer adds a $199 product to an online shopping cart. The checkout page displays the correct amount, and the payment gateway is functioning normally. Before submitting the checkout request, the customer manipulates the payment amount and changes it to $1. Before submitting the checkout request, they manipulate the payment amount and change it to $1. If the backend trusts that modified amount instead of retrieving the actual product price from its own database, the customer could potentially complete the purchase for just $1. The payment provider might successfully authorize the transaction. The checkout could display a successful payment confirmation. Yet the merchant would receive the wrong amount. items.title: Your coding agent keeps writing the same UI. Give it real components instead
items.summary: Ask a coding agent for a pricing section and you get the same pricing section everyone else gets: three cards, the middle one highlighted, a gradient somewhere. Agents write UI from memory, and their memory averages out to a template. Good UI code is already out there, free to use. shadcn/ui, Radix, Base UI, Magic UI, Kokonut UI, Aceternity UI and the shadcn-style registries around them have components that someone designed, tested and shipped. The agent just doesn't know where to look, and searching 40 sites by hand is not something you want to do for every screen. We built Clay UI for that gap. It is an MIT-licensed CLI plus an agent skill. Your agent asks it for a component, picks from real matches, downloads the source and then rewrites it to fit your project. Install it in a project: npx @behavio1/clayui init This installs a skill for Claude Code (and for Codex, Cursor and other agents that read .agents/skills) and builds a local index of the libraries. After that you talk to your agent as usual: Find me a data table with filters and make it match our dashboard. The agent runs a search. items.title: What a Node.js App Needs Before You Deploy It (with a ShardCloud Walkthrough)
items.summary: Your Express app runs fine with node index.js on your laptop. Then you deploy it and you get a 502, an app that never finishes starting, or an app that dies every few hours. Most of the time the code is fine. The app just assumes things that are true on your machine and false inside a container. This post covers those assumptions first, as a checklist you can use on any platform. Then it walks through a real deploy on ShardCloud, so you can see where each item shows up. Platforms decide which port your app listens on and pass it in as PORT. A hardcoded 3000 is the most common reason a deploy "works" in the logs but returns 502. const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000; Keep the fallback so node index.js still works locally. 0.0.0.0, not localhost Inside a container, localhost means "only reachable from inside this container". The platform's proxy sits outside it, so it can't reach an app bound to 127.0.0.1. app.listen(port, "0.0.0.0", () => { console.log(`Listening on ${port}`); }); Express binds to all interfaces when you pass no host. items.title: TypeScript Path Aliases Work in the Editor but Fail at Runtime: tsc-alias vs Subpath Imports vs a Bundler
items.summary: TypeScript's paths option only teaches the type checker where to look; tsc does not rewrite the import specifiers in the JavaScript it emits. So import { db } from "@/lib/db" compiles cleanly, then Node throws Cannot find module '@/lib/db'. You can fix it by rewriting aliases after compile (tsc-alias), by switching to Node's native subpath imports (#lib/*), by bundling, or by running through a tool that resolves paths itself (tsx). Here is the setup that trips people up: { "compilerOptions": { "baseUrl": ".", "paths": { "@/*": ["src/*"] }, "outDir": "dist", "module": "commonjs" } } // src/server.ts import { db } from "@/lib/db"; tsc succeeds, autocomplete works, and then: $ node dist/server.js Error: Cannot find module '@/lib/db' Require stack: - /app/dist/server.js (With ESM output the message reads ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND / Cannot find package '@', because Node treats @/lib/db as a scoped package name.) If you open dist/server.js, the specifier is still @/lib/db. The TypeScript team has long treated this as intentional: paths describes how some other tool will resolve modules at runtime, and the compiler does not transform import text. items.title: This try/catch Doesn't Catch: The Promise Mistake That Crashes Node
items.summary: Quick quiz. Does the catch block run? async function loadDashboard() { try { const userP = getUser(); // takes 300 ms, succeeds const ordersP = getOrders(); // fails after 100 ms const user = await userP; const orders = await ordersP; return { user, orders }; } catch (err) { console.log('caught:', err.message); } } Both requests start in parallel, everything is inside try, and the error should land in catch. Take a guess before you scroll. 👇 . . . No. In Node 22 the process dies with exit code 1, and caught: is never printed: Error: orders failed Node.js v22.19.0 Node has a simple rule. When a promise rejects, it lets the current batch of microtasks finish, then checks whether anything handles the rejection. If nothing does, it raises an unhandled rejection. Since Node 15 the default is to treat that like an uncaught exception, and the process exits. await attaches a handler, but only to the promise you're currently awaiting, and only when execution reaches that line: time what happens 0 ms both requests start; await userP attaches a handler to userP only 100 ms ordersP rejects, and nothing is handling it → crash 300 ms userP resolves; await ordersP would attach the handler now. items.summary: A logistics pricing rollout needs enough evidence to reverse a bad decision, but recording every flag evaluation can turn an operational safeguard into an unbounded data set. Short answer: implement feature flags in Node.js behind a dedicated decision module, retrieve their state through a supported API or client, and retain a bounded record of each pricing decision before expanding exposure. Budget evidence around three things: label cardinality, retention, and sampling. Rollback safety determines what survives each budget. The concrete job is introducing a new shipping-price rule behind a flag while preserving the ability to return new quotes to the previous rule. A shipment notification adds a second question: did the associated message send? Those questions need a shared decision identifier, but neither requires a shipment identifier on every metric series. Start with the business boundary. A flag selects which pricing rule produces a quote. The decision module should return that selection to the quoting code once, and the quote should preserve the rule version that actually ran. items.title: Obfuscating a JSON source-generated context
items.summary: A [JsonSerializable] context is the serializer you reach for when you are about to obfuscate. The reflection-based path reads your live property names at runtime, so renaming CustomerRef to a turns your JSON into {"a":…}; the source-generated path resolves everything at compile time and reaches your members through typed delegates, so the rename is invisible on the wire. That much is well known. What is less obvious is how the generated context stays intact — and where it does not. The generator writes the serialization contract down in two kinds of thing: tokens that the renamer follows, and literals that it leaves exactly where they are. A source-generated JsonSerializerContext is rename-safe precisely when those two halves stay in step, and it desyncs the moment a code path sidesteps the context. So the question worth answering concretely is: what does the generator actually emit, which parts move under renaming and which do not, and how do you prove the halves still line up after Nebula runs? items.title: How I Stopped Passcode Brute-Force From Freezing Live Keystrokes in Carrel
items.summary: When I started building Carrel, a real-time collaborative CodeMirror 6 workspace, I thought auth was the easy part: hash room passcodes with scrypt, verify on join, done. Then I tested what happens under brute-force traffic. scrypt is slow on purpose. Run it synchronously and it blocks Node's event loop; run dozens of async scrypt calls uncapped and they saturate libuv's threadpool. Either way, anyone hammering wrong passcodes starts stuttering live keystrokes for everyone typing in the room. Here is how I ended up structuring the server and protocol across the 3-package TypeScript monorepo (@carrel/shared, @carrel/server, @carrel/client): In server/src/throttle.ts, POST /api/rooms/:id/ticket runs async scrypt inside a 4-slot concurrency limiter paired with per-IP progressive lockouts (and ignores X-Forwarded-For unless TRUST_PROXY is explicitly enabled). Once verified, the client gets a short-lived, single-use nonce-bound HMAC ticket to upgrade /ws, which gets burned immediately on upgrade so replay attempts fail. items.summary: Next.js 16.4.4 shipped a backported fix that puts the CSP nonce on the Partial Prerendering (PPR) resume bootstrap, the small inline script that wakes up the dynamic part of a prerendered page. If you run a strict, nonce based Content Security Policy on top of PPR, that script has to carry the nonce your policy expects, or the browser is supposed to block it. Here's how I'd reproduce the problem on your current version, prove the patch fixes it on yours, and wire a check into CI so it never sneaks back. TL;DR 16.4.4 is a patch release with two backports: a Turbopack startup CSS update fix and the CSP nonce fix for the PPR resume bootstrap. It is not the canary feature set, so don't upgrade expecting anything else. A nonce only protects you if every script the framework emits carries it. Verify that against the raw HTML and in a real browser, not by reading the release note. Put a two part check in CI: every executable script in the HTML has the response nonce, and a headless browser reports zero CSP violations on your PPR routes. items.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
items.summary: Hi HN! I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious. So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves. I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back! items.title: Your Upgrade Passed Every Test. Your API Docs Still Broke.
items.summary: After moving a project to .NET 11, everything was green. Build, tests, app startup. Then the Swagger UI page refused to render. The cause is one default. OpenApiOptions.OpenApiVersion now defaults to OpenAPI 3.2 instead of 3.1, so /openapi/v1.json starts with "openapi": "3.2.0". The server returns 200 and logs nothing. The swagger-ui bundled in Swashbuckle.AspNetCore.SwaggerUI 10.1.4 and earlier only understands 3.0 and 3.1, so it gives up. Your tests won't catch this, because the server isn't broken. The contract format changed, and the people who notice are your consumers: client generators, gateway imports, someone else's contract tests. The full article covers: three fixes: update the UI package, pin to 3.1, or serve a 3.2 and a 3.1 document side by side (plus the ShouldInclude line that side-by-side setup needs) why pinning down to 3.0 swaps one breaking change for another what breaks in custom document and schema transformers after the move to Microsoft.OpenApi 3.x a five-minute test that fails your pipeline the next time a framework upgrade changes the document version Read the full article on Medium

items.title: React Component Lifecycle & useEffect
items.summary: Have you ever wondered what happens when a React component is created, updated, or removed from the screen? React components go through different stages during their lifetime. These stages are known as the Component Lifecycle. In modern React, the useEffect() hook helps us perform tasks such as fetching data, updating the document title, setting timers, and handling event listeners. What is the Component Lifecycle in React? The component lifecycle refers to the different stages a component goes through from the moment it appears on the screen until it is removed. A React component generally goes through three important stages: Mounting – The component is created and displayed on the screen. Updating – The component re-renders when its state or props change. Unmounting – The component is removed from the screen. 1. Mounting Phase Mounting is the stage when a component is created and displayed for the first time. For example, when we open a webpage and a React component appears on the screen, the component is in its mounting phase. items.title: Building Market Chart From Scratch: An Open-Source Financial Charting Engine
items.summary: Building Market Chart From Scratch: An Open-Source Financial Charting Engine What does it take to build a financial charting library from scratch? Not just rendering candlesticks. A serious market charting engine needs to handle rendering performance, large datasets, real-time updates, technical indicators, interactive drawing tools, multiple chart types, persistence, and much more. I wanted to explore these engineering challenges by building an independent charting engine rather than relying entirely on an existing charting solution. That's how Market Chart started. items.title: React Interview Questions and Answers (2026)
items.summary: Originally published on nostrobeai.com. React interviews concentrate on a predictable core: the virtual DOM and reconciliation, state versus props, the hook rules and why they exist, why lists need stable keys, and how to avoid unnecessary re-renders. Most questions are testing whether you understand the mental model rather than whether you have memorised an API — an interviewer asking about keys wants to hear about reconciliation, not about avoiding a console warning. Be ready to explain why a rule exists, not just what it says, and to name the trade-off in any performance optimisation you propose, since useMemo and useCallback both cost something. Below are the common questions, with concise answers you can adapt in your own words. The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and applies the minimal set of real DOM updates. This avoids expensive, manual DOM manipulation and lets you write declarative UI as a function of state. items.title: Letting a coding agent on Linux build, test and debug an iOS app
items.summary: I run Claude Code and Codex on a Linux machine. For web and backend work that's fine. For iOS it breaks down fast: there's no Xcode on Linux, no simulator, so the agent writes Swift it can never compile, and I end up being the compiler, copying errors back and forth. I built a small tool for that, called box. This post is about what I learned making a remote Mac useful to an agent, not to a human. (Disclosure: box is my product, it's paid, and the link is at the end.) A human can scroll through a 2,000-line xcodebuild log and find the one red line. An agent burns context doing that and often fixes the wrong thing. What worked better was making each build return something short and structured: $ box build box: 1 compile error(s): App/Module0.swift:2:19: cannot convert value of type 'String' to specified type 'Int' 1 | import Foundation > 2 | let broken: Int = "x" 3 | struct Module0 { box: bj_5WO8cgwGaPXkXTit failed, 60s billed Tests come back the same way, as a count plus files the agent can open: $ box test box: tests 3 passed, 0 failed box: saved ./.box/out/bj_f-P-JW-6hWjR-OnA/test-summary.json box: saved ./.box/out/bj_f-P-JW-6hWjR-OnA/test.xcresult.zip box: bj_f-P-JW-6hWjR-OnA su

items.title: Blocking an order because a server is down is worse than not checking at all
items.summary: Clinical decision support at order time sounds simple. A physician places an order, a service checks it against the patient record, and the screen either confirms the order or offers alternatives. In practice the check has to meet three requirements at once: it runs inside the ordering screen the physician already uses, it answers fast enough not to break their train of thought, and it gives a reason rather than a bare refusal. Almost every hard decision in this kind of integration follows from those three. The call sits inside a synchronous workflow, so a slow or missing answer is not a background problem. It is a physician waiting. That means: A strict timeout on every call A defined fail-open path, because blocking an order when the service is unreachable is the worse outcome A log entry for every fail-open, so the gap is visible afterwards instead of silent Firing on marginal cases trains clinicians to dismiss everything, including the alerts that matter. Tune the evoke conditions, the rules for when a module runs, rather than polishing the wording of the warning. items.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. By chaining fast in-memory process caching, a Redis caching tier, and a high-RAM SQL Server database, they rendered pages in 20 milliseconds by eliminating distributed network latency. I miss the era when Stack Overflow was the undisputed center of our engineering world. At the time, they were serving roughly 200 million requests a day on just nine on-premise web servers running a monolithic .NET stack. In fact, they pointed out that they could have technically powered the entire site on a single machine, though nobody would recommend running without redundancy. items.title: Compiling F# Directly to WebAssembly GC Without the .NET Runtime
items.summary: For years, running F# in the browser or on edge platforms has come with a familiar trade-off: you ship the entire .NET runtime alongside your code. Solutions like Blazor and Uno are capable, but they carry multi-megabyte payloads and noticeable startup overhead—both of which hurt when you are targeting fast web apps or resource-constrained edge isolates. With modern WebAssembly features now standardized across major engines—specifically WasmGC, Tail Calls, Exception Handling, and JS String Builtins—compilers for functional languages no longer need to bundle their own garbage collector or linear-memory runtime. Over the past months, I have been building fsharp-wasm, an experimental open-source compiler and ecosystem (licensed under Apache-2.0) that compiles F# directly into WasmGC binaries without the .NET runtime or Base Class Library (BCL). items.title: I gave Claude's voice a hologram face: a free, open-source macOS app
items.summary: Inspired by Joi, the hologram from Blade Runner 2049, I built Visage: a small macOS app that gives a hologram face to the voice of the AI you already talk to. Start Claude's voice mode (or ChatGPT's), and a face floats on your desktop and speaks with that voice: lips in sync, alive between sentences. It listens while you talk, thinks once you have finished, then answers. It is free and open source (MIT), and macOS only (macOS 15 or later, Apple silicon and Intel). No API key, no server, no account. Visage never talks to the AI app: it taps the sound that app plays with a per-process Core Audio tap, mutes it, and plays it back itself about 150 ms later. That delay is the trick. The voice analysis has already "heard" what comes next, so the lips can move before the sound, the way a real speaker's do, instead of trailing behind it. In a conversation, 150 ms more before the answer goes unnoticed. Voice analysis without a model: energy, pitch (YIN), formants (LPC), fricatives and lip closures, in plain signal processing with Accelerate. items.title: “Available Offline.” On Which Device? Testing Offline Maps on Apple Watch
items.summary: Your iPhone finishes downloading the trail map. You leave it in the car. Two kilometers up the trail, you reach a fork and check your Apple Watch. The route line is there. Underneath it, an empty grid. Which way do you turn? I’d start with the same action a hiker takes: download a route on the iPhone and wait until the app says “Available offline.” Then I’d leave the iPhone behind, take the Watch offline, and open the route on the Watch for the first time. That last detail matters. If I open the map while I’m still at my desk, I may only prove that the Watch can display an area it loaded a minute ago. On the Watch, I’d check three things: At the fork: Can I see the junction and both branches clearly enough to choose a trail? Farther along: If I pan to a section I’ve never viewed and zoom in, does the map still draw underneath the route? After reopening the app: Can I get back to the same offline map with the phone still out of reach? I’d give the iPhone and the Watch separate download states. “Downloaded on iPhone” tells me what has finished. “Ready on Apple Watch” is a promise I’d make only after the Watch has verified that it can open the saved map. items.summary: For a new iPhone app in 2026, I start in SwiftUI and reach for UIKit only where SwiftUI still falls short. Most of my work as a freelance iOS developer is SwiftUI. It isn't an either-or choice: the two mix in one app, so the question is which one leads. Widgets are built with SwiftUI views through WidgetKit, and so are Live Activities on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island (Apple). One codebase across Apple's platforms: the same views run on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Vision Pro, with platform tweaks. Less code for the same screen: layouts, state and animation are declared, not wired by hand, so screens are quicker to build and to change. Rich text editing and other text work beyond what SwiftUI's text views offer. Very custom scrolling and list layouts, where you need control over every cell and every offset. Large existing UIKit apps, where rewriting working screens buys nothing. Libraries that only ship UIKit views, such as some SDKs for maps, video or ads. UIViewRepresentable and UIViewControllerRepresentable put a UIKit view inside a SwiftUI screen. items.title: NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features
items.summary: The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. Read more of this story

items.title: Plato's Key (8 minute read)
items.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that neural networks converge toward a shared representation of reality. Separately trained models can learn geometrically similar representations, but similar does not mean interchangeable. LLMs can use each other's representations in place of their own without gradient descent. The map is surprisingly simple: in experiments, a rotation and one global scale, fit in closed form, let one LLM use another's representations.

items.title: Measuring RSI (12 minute read)
items.summary: Neither compute allocation nor human intervention measures whether an AI training algorithm improved. Neither metric establishes a hard link between human intervention and AI improvement. Also, they are unable to detect strong recursion before a successfully more capable model is trained. Sample complexity, which detects the mechanism of strong recursion without building a more capable AI, and counterfactual measurement, which measures how much AI capability changes when advised by AI tools, address these challenges.

items.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps. items.title: Physicists Send an Unblockable Message Using Gravity
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from Phys.org: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances. "Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." items.title: World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. items.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
items.summary: The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.

items.title: Switching LLMs mid-conversation is a ski-rental problem (30 minute read)

items.title: Unblockable communication with gravity (32 minute read)
